questions.q: Phenol is treated with NaOH, the salt is heated with CO₂ at about 125 °C and 100 atm, and the product is acidified. The final product is:
questions.explain: In Kolbe's reaction the –COOH enters ortho to the OH of sodium phenoxide, giving salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) after acidification.

questions.q: Why is phenol converted into its phenoxide before reaction with CO₂ in Kolbe's reaction?
options: Phenoxide is much more electron-rich and can attack the weak electrophile CO₂
Phenoxide protects the OH group from carboxylation
CO₂ reacts only with ionic compounds
Phenol would be oxidised by CO₂
questions.explain: CO₂ is a weak electrophile. The negative charge of phenoxide is delocalised into the ring, making the ortho and para carbons nucleophilic enough to attack it; phenol itself is not reactive enough.

questions.q: If KOH is used instead of NaOH in the Kolbe–Schmitt reaction, the product favoured is:
questions.explain: Potassium phenoxide pushes the carboxyl group to the para position and is used industrially for 4-hydroxybenzoic acid. Sodium phenoxide gives mainly the ortho acid.

questions.q: Phenol → (i) NaOH (ii) CO₂, 125 °C, 100 atm (iii) H₃O⁺ (iv) (CH₃CO)₂O, H⁺. The final product is:
questions.explain: Steps (i)–(iii) give salicylic acid, and acetylation of its OH with acetic anhydride gives acetylsalicylic acid. 4-Acetoxybenzoic acid would need the para acid from the potassium route.
